prompt: Every app server health check queries the shared primary database. During a 20-second database failover, the balancer marks a backend unhealthy after two probes 5 seconds apart and is configured to fail closed when all are unhealthy. What can happen, and how can the design improve?

options.text: Nothing bad; the balancer just waits for the database
options.explanation: The balancer doesn't know about the database. It sees every backend failing its health check and removes them all.

options.text: Only one backend fails, so traffic moves to the others
options.explanation: All backends share the same database, so they all fail the same check at the same moment. There's nowhere to move traffic to.

options.text: The balancer automatically switches to the database replica
options.explanation: Load balancers in front of app servers don't manage database connections; failing over the database is a separate mechanism.

options.text: All backends can be marked unhealthy together, so this fail-closed balancer also rejects database-independent requests. Separate shared-dependency handling from readiness and choose fail-open policy deliberately.
options.explanation: Correct. A deep dependency check turns a shared-dependency blip into a total outage. Check local health (process, thread pool, ability to respond) for readiness, handle dependency failures per request, and rely on fail-open or panic thresholds as a safety net.

workedExample:
1. The shared database is unavailable for 20 seconds. The stated 5-second/two-failure checks can mark all app servers unhealthy before recovery.
2. This fail-closed balancer then rejects even requests that do not use the database.
3. Recovery checks can prolong the visible outage.
4. Design readiness around the traffic each instance can actually serve, handle dependency failures per request, and explicitly choose fail-open versus fail-closed.
5. Product behavior differs: AWS ALB fails open when all registered targets are unhealthy; Envoy has a configurable panic threshold.

prompt: An active checker starts a probe every 10 seconds and marks a backend unhealthy after three failures. Assume probe failures and state changes are instantaneous. One of ten backends, receiving 200 requests/s, crashes just after a passing check. With no retries or passive checks, roughly how many requests fail before removal?

options.explanation: That's one second's worth of traffic. Detection takes three failed probes 10 s apart, so it's closer to 30 s.
Correct. Three 10 s probe intervals give about 30 s of detection delay. At 200 requests per second to the dead backend, that leaves about 6,000 failed requests.
That would be the whole fleet's traffic (2,000 rps) for 30 s. Only the dead backend's share fails.

options.text: None, because the balancer notices instantly
options.explanation: Active checks only notice at the next probe; the balancer has no instant signal unless passive outlier detection is enabled.

workedExample:
```formula
t_detect ≈ interval × threshold
t_detect ≈ 10 s × 3 = 30 s
N_fail ≈ t_detect × r
N_fail ≈ 30 s × 200 rps = 6,000
where
t_detect: the worst-case time until the balancer marks the dead backend unhealthy (it crashed just after a pass), in seconds (s)
interval: the time between probes, 10 s
threshold: the unhealthy threshold, 3 consecutive failed probes
N_fail: the number of requests sent to the dead backend before removal
r: the request rate to that backend, 200 requests per second (rps)
s: second
rps: requests per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: three failed probes 10 s apart take 30 s, and 30 s of that backend's traffic is about 6,000 failed requests.
```

Ways to shrink it:
  - **Passive outlier detection:** eject after, say, 5 consecutive 5xx or connection failures, potentially quickly after completed failures accumulate; connection or request timeouts can delay those signals.
  - **Retries** of idempotent requests to another backend.
  - Shorter intervals, at the cost of more probe traffic.

link.title: Health checks for target groups (AWS ALB)

prompt: An Envoy cluster has one priority, ten equally weighted backends, no degraded or excluded hosts, and default fail-open panic behavior. Six fail health checks and four are healthy; the panic threshold is 50%. How does it route?

options.explanation: That's what happens while at least 50% of hosts are healthy. Here only 40% are, which is below the threshold.

options.text: It returns 503 to every request until more backends recover
options.explanation: Panic mode exists to avoid exactly that. Envoy keeps serving rather than failing everything.

options.text: It sends all traffic to a single backend
options.explanation: Nothing in Envoy's behaviour concentrates traffic on one host in this situation.

options.text: Across all 10 backends, ignoring health status, because healthy hosts (40%) are below the 50% panic threshold
options.explanation: Correct. Envoy assumes that when most hosts look unhealthy, the health checks themselves may be wrong, or the healthy few would be overwhelmed. Some requests fail, but roughly 40% succeed instead of risking a total collapse.

workedExample:
```formula
f_healthy = n_healthy / n_total
f_healthy = 4 / 10 = 40%
f_healthy < T_panic = 50%
where
f_healthy: the fraction of hosts currently passing health checks
n_healthy: healthy hosts, 4
n_total: all hosts in the cluster, 10
T_panic: Envoy's panic threshold, 50% by default
<: less than
%: per cent
In words: only 40% of hosts look healthy, below the 50% threshold, so Envoy enters panic mode.
```

1. 40% < 50% → **panic mode**.
2. In panic mode, Envoy balances across **all** hosts as if they were healthy.
3. Expected success ≈ 40% of requests (those reaching good hosts), versus the risk that 4 hosts receiving 100% of the load fall over too.
4. Trade-off: if the 6 really are dead, you serve some errors; if the checks are wrong, you avoid a self-inflicted outage.
